common_name: Sogo Yukidian Moth Orchid (Award-Winning Cascading White Phalaenopsis)

planting.note: Repot after flowering finishes and new root growth resumes, spacing repots roughly every one to two years as bark breaks down.

directions: This Taiwan-bred grex produces long, arching sprays densely shingled with pure white, waxy flowers up to five inches across, among the showiest cascading Phalaenopsis in cultivation. Grow in bright, curtain-filtered light with no direct midday sun, in fine fir bark or sphagnum that holds slight moisture between waterings. Its dense, waterfall-like bloom habit and pure white color without any pink or yellow flush distinguish it from most novelty-colored Phalaenopsis hybrids. Keep humidity above 50 percent and maintain steady warmth, since cool drafts can cause bud blast on the long spikes.

common_name: Kenneth Schubert Doritaenopsis (Lavender-Blue Primary Hybrid Moth Orchid)

planting.note: Repot after bloom into fresh fine bark once roots begin actively growing, generally every one to two years.

directions: A classic 1963 primary hybrid between Doritis pulcherrima and Phalaenopsis violacea, this grex carries dozens of small, slightly fragrant lavender-blue flowers on multiple branching spikes, a foundation parent behind much of the modern purple and blue Phalaenopsis breeding line. Grow warm and humid in fine bark or sphagnum with bright, filtered light, watering as the medium approaches dryness. Its compact growth and multi-flowered branching spikes set it apart from standard large-flowered Phalaenopsis, and its stronger sun tolerance reflects its Doritis parentage. Widely sold under the trade name Doritaenopsis even though modern taxonomy folds Doritis into Phalaenopsis.

common_name: Yip Sum Wah Ascocenda (Classic Orange-Red Compact Vanda Hybrid)

planting.note: Mount or basket-culture with exposed roots; repot or remount only when the basket deteriorates, since Vanda-alliance roots resent disturbance.

directions: One of the most widely grown Ascocenda hybrids since its 1965 registration, Yip Sum Wah bears rounded, waxy flowers in shades from orange and flame-red to deep crimson on upright spikes, and has produced dozens of AOS-awarded color-form cultivars. Grow in a slatted basket or mounted with roots exposed to air, in strong light and high humidity typical of Vanda-alliance culture, watering or misting daily in warm weather. Its compact plant size relative to full Vanda species, paired with the rounded flower shape, makes it a favorite intermediate between miniature Ascocentrum and large Vanda. Ascocentrum has been botanically folded into Vanda, but the Ascocenda trade name remains standard in cultivation.

common_name: Hawaiian Wedding Song Cattleya (Fragrant White Cut-Flower Orchid)

planting.note: Repot every two to three years just as new root growth begins after a flowering cycle.

directions: Registered in 1982 as a cross of Cattleya Angel Bells and Cattleya Claesiana, this fragrant hybrid produces elegant, snow-white flowers roughly four inches across that last six to eight weeks, making it a long-standing favorite among cut-flower and wedding-bouquet growers, typically blooming twice yearly in summer and again in late winter. Grow in bright, filtered light in coarse bark mix, allowing the medium to approach dryness between thorough waterings. Its pure white color, heavy fragrance, and unusually long-lasting blooms distinguish it from most compact modern Cattleya hybrids bred primarily for color. Sometimes listed under the segregate genus Rhyncholaeliocattleya in older nursery catalogs.

common_name: Enobi Purple Dendrobium (Magenta-and-White Hard-Cane Hybrid Orchid)

planting.note: Divide and repot mature multi-cane clumps in spring once new growths show active roots.

directions: A 1996 hard-cane hybrid between Dendrobium Enobi Komachi and Dendrobium Laguna Princess, this widely grown Japanese-bred grex carries twelve or more bright magenta-purple flowers with a darker throat in succession along upright to semi-pendulous spikes on fleshy cane-type pseudobulbs. Grow warm with bright indirect light, watering regularly during active summer growth and allowing canes to dry more between waterings in cooler months to encourage bud set rather than keiki growth. Its dense, evenly spaced flower count and clean magenta-and-white coloring distinguish it from the more open-flowered nobile-type Dendrobium hybrids common in home cultivation.

common_name: Titanic Zygopetalum (Tall Fragrant Hyacinth-Scented Orchid Hybrid)

planting.note: Repot in fresh open mix after the late-fall to winter bloom cycle finishes, dividing congested pseudobulb clumps.

directions: Bred in Australia in 1986 from Zygopetalum John Banks crossed with Zygopetalum B.G. White, this taller-growing hybrid sends up flower spikes eighteen to twenty-four inches tall carrying heavily hyacinth-scented, green-and-purple mottled blooms that last six to eight weeks in late fall through winter. Grow in intermediate to cool temperatures with medium to bright light and evenly moist, well-drained bark-based media, since Zygopetalum roots dislike drying out completely. Its notably tall spikes and strong hyacinth fragrance set it apart from the more compact Zygopetalum hybrids already common in cultivation. Repeat spring flowering is common on well-established plants.

common_name: Winston Churchill Slipper Orchid (Historic Red-and-Spotted Paphiopedilum Hybrid)

planting.note: Repot annually to every other year in fine, fast-draining mix, since Paphiopedilum lacks pseudobulbs for water storage.

directions: Registered in 1951 from a cross of Paphiopedilum Eridge and Paphiopedilum Hampden, this hybrid is one of the most influential slipper orchid crosses ever made, with its award-winning red-and-white spotted cultivars still standing behind much of modern standard Paphiopedilum breeding. Flowers show a rounded dorsal sepal heavily overlaid with maroon-red spotting above mottled or plain green foliage depending on the cultivar line. Grow in bright shade in a fine bark-and-perlite mix kept evenly moist but never soggy, since these terrestrial orchids have no pseudobulbs to buffer drought. Its historic breeding significance and dense red spotting pattern distinguish it from the paler or more solid-colored Paphiopedilum hybrids already common in cultivation.

common_name: Chocolate Drop Cattleya (Dark Red Citrus-Scented Cluster Orchid)

planting.note: Repot into a slightly larger bark pot every two to three years once new roots emerge from fresh growths.

directions: A 1965 primary hybrid between Cattleya guttata and Guarianthe aurantiaca, this vigorous grex produces dense clusters of small, waxy, dark red and burgundy flowers with a yellow-blending throat, capable of specimen plants with hundreds of blooms open at once, plus a distinctive light, sharp citrus fragrance. Grow in bright light with good air movement in coarse bark, watering thoroughly and letting the mix approach dryness between waterings. Its cluster-type inflorescence and citrus scent set it apart from the larger single-flowered Cattleya hybrids and species already in cultivation, and it remains a widely used parent for dark red progeny. Sometimes listed as Cattlianthe Chocolate Drop following reclassification of its Guarianthe parent.

common_name: Peter Pan Greensleeves Cymbidium (Compact Tetraploid Green Miniature Orchid)

planting.note: Divide and repot after late-winter to spring bloom once the plant has finished flowering.

directions: Bred in 1957 from a cross of Cymbidium ensifolium and Cymbidium Miretta, this compact miniature grex produces upright spikes of rounded green flowers in late winter through spring, with the tetraploid 'Greensleeves' cultivar prized for its clean color and vigorous, free-flowering habit. Grow cool with bright, filtered light, watering roughly weekly in summer and less often in winter, and allow a modest day-night temperature drop in autumn to trigger reliable spiking. Its compact, miniature plant size compared to standard large-flowered Cymbidium hybrids makes it far better suited to windowsill or small-greenhouse culture. Repot in a bark-and-perlite mix, dividing congested bulb clumps after flowering.

common_name: Robert's Delight Vanda (Award-Winning Compact Blue-to-Red Vanda Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow basket- or slab-mounted with roots exposed; repot or remount only as the mounting medium breaks down.

directions: Bred by R.F. Orchids in 1984 from Vanda Kasem's Delight crossed with Vanda Madame Rattana, this hybrid has produced numerous AOS-awarded color forms ranging from deep blue and black-purple to red and pink, all with the large, flat, rounded flower shape typical of strap-leaf Vanda breeding. Grow in strong light with high humidity and daily watering or misting in warm weather, letting roots dry briefly between soakings. Its compact plant habit relative to full-size species Vanda, combined with its wide color range within a single grex, distinguishes it from the more narrowly colored Vanda hybrids already in cultivation. Best grown in a slatted basket or mounted to allow full root aeration.

common_name: Lycaena Pansy Orchid (Historic Near-Red Miltoniopsis Hybrid)

planting.note: Repot annually into fresh fine bark or sphagnum, since Miltoniopsis is intolerant of stale, broken-down media.

directions: Registered in 1925 from a cross of Miltoniopsis Lord Lambourne and Miltoniopsis Princess Margaret, this historic hybrid was among the first Miltoniopsis grexes to achieve a nearly solid red flower without the pale waterfall mask pattern typical of earlier hybrids, and it remains an influential ancestor behind modern red and burgundy pansy orchid breeding. Grow cool with bright, indirect light, keeping the fine bark or sphagnum medium evenly moist and humidity above 60 percent, since Miltoniopsis roots are thin and drought-sensitive. Its pioneering near-solid red coloring distinguishes it from the pink, white, and blotched-pattern Miltoniopsis hybrids already common in cultivation.

common_name: Eternal Wind Spider Orchid (Fragrant Lime-Yellow Compact Brassia Hybrid)

planting.note: Repot after flowering once new growths show active roots, dividing large pseudobulb clumps every few years.

directions: Bred in Japan in 1993 from Brassia Bracdiana crossed with Brassia Rex, this compact spider orchid hybrid carries long, narrow lime-yellow petals patterned with dark brown blotches on a broader similarly marked lip, with a spicy-sweet fragrance noticeable from early morning into the afternoon. Grow in bright, filtered light in a well-drained bark mix, watering freely during active growth and allowing a slight dry-down between waterings, particularly in cooler months. Its notably compact habit and short flower spikes held close above the foliage make it easier to manage as a houseplant than larger species-type Brassia, distinguishing it from the taller spider orchids already in the collection.
